entries.label: Round and square brackets swapped for the inequality signs
entries.description: The student gets the end numbers right but pairs the bracket at a finite end with the wrong sign, writing a square bracket for $<$ or $>$, or a round bracket for $\le$ or $\ge$, so an end number is wrongly kept or wrongly left out.
entries.signal: A bracket in the final answer does not match the sign at that end, for example $(-13, 4]$ written for $-13\le x<4$, or $21<x\le41$ written for $[21, 41)$.

refutation.text_md: You have the right two numbers in the right order, and you are matching each bracket to an inequality sign, which is the right idea. The slip is which bracket goes with which sign: a square bracket has landed on a $<$ or $>$, or a round bracket on a $\le$ or $\ge$.

In the book's answers, $\le$ and $\ge$ go with a square bracket, and $<$ and $>$ go with a round bracket. For example $-13\le x<4$ is written $[-13, 4)$: square at $-13$ because of the $\le$, round at $4$ because of the $<$.

Swap them and you have written a different set. $(-13, 4]$ leaves out $-13$ and keeps $4$, which is $-13<x\le4$. The set in the question keeps $-13$ and leaves out $4$, so the swapped answer is wrong at both ends.

Check each end on its own, using only the sign at that end: $\le$ or $\ge$ gets a square bracket, $<$ or $>$ gets a round bracket. Going the other way, read the bracket the same way: in $[21, 41)$ the square bracket gives $21\le x$ and the round bracket gives $x<41$. When one end runs on for ever, as in $x\le7$, write $-\infty$ with a round bracket and let the $7$ follow its sign: $(-\infty, 7]$.

verdict.reason: I worked every claim against the canonical solutions. The pairing is right: [-13,4) is -13<=x<4 and (-inf,7] is x<=7. The two examples are right: (-13,4] is -13<x<=4, so it is wrong at both ends, and [21,41) is 21<=x<41, so its swap is 21<x<=41. The refutation argues against the swapped pairing, not just the method. Step 4 stays within the canonical answers. 'In the book's answers' is generic and gives no id, page or figure. The signal is concrete and would not misdiagnose a student.

entries.label: Interval notation used for a set that is not an interval of real numbers
entries.description: The student takes brackets to mean just 'from this number to that one' and writes interval notation for a set that is not every real number between two ends, such as one that holds only some of the numbers in that stretch.

refutation.text_md: You are right that a bracket pair such as $(-5, 5)$ says 'from $-5$ to $5$'. What it also says is that the set holds every real number in that stretch, not just the whole numbers or a chosen few.
That is why the set notation for $(-5, 5)$ reads $\{k:k\in\mathbb{R},-5<k<5\}$. The part $k\in\mathbb{R}$ says $k$ can be any real number, so $0.5$ and $-4.99$ are in the set just as $0$ and $3$ are.

So if a set leaves out some of the real numbers between its two ends, for example because it holds only whole numbers, it is not an interval of real numbers. Writing it with brackets would wrongly add every number it leaves out, and the book's caution is that interval notation can only be used to represent an interval of real numbers.

Before you write brackets, check that the set is described with $\in\mathbb{R}$ and inequalities, like $\{p:p\in\mathbb{R},p\le6\}$, which becomes $(-\infty, 6]$. Going the other way, keep the $x\in\mathbb{R}$ part in your set notation, like $\{x:x\in\mathbb{R},x>35\}$ for $(35, \infty)$.

verdict.reason: The book's caution says interval notation can only represent an interval of real numbers, and that directly supports the error. The refutation checks out. (-5,5) matches {k:k in R,-5<k<5}, and {p:p in R,p<=6} becomes (-inf,6] while {x:x in R,x>35} is (35,inf). The whole-numbers example correctly shows that brackets would add the missing reals. It argues against the error and teaches nothing beyond the caution and the canonical set forms. 'The book's caution' is a generic mention with no id or page. The entry has no signal, so signal_ok is true.

entries.label: Square bracket written next to infinity
entries.description: The student treats $\infty$ or $-\infty$ like an end number that can be included, so writes a square bracket next to it, as in $[-\infty, 5]$ or $[5, \infty]$.
entries.signal: A square bracket sitting directly beside $\infty$ or $-\infty$, such as $[-\infty, 5]$ or $[5, \infty]$.

refutation.text_md: Giving every end of an interval a bracket, and using a square one when the end is included, is the right idea. The slip is treating $\infty$ or $-\infty$ as one more end number that can be included.

Set notation lists the numbers an interval holds: every $x$ with $x\in\mathbb{R}$ that meets the condition. A square bracket says the end itself is one of those numbers. But $\infty$ is not a real number. It only says the numbers keep going and never stop, so there is no end number there to include.

Take the real numbers $x$ with $x\le7$. Its interval is $(-\infty, 7]$. The square bracket sits at $7$, because $\le$ includes $7$. Writing $[-\infty, 7]$ would claim that $-\infty$ is one of the numbers in the set, and it is not.

Choose the bracket at a number end from the sign: $<$ or $>$ gives a round bracket, $\le$ or $\ge$ gives a square one. The $\infty$ end has no number to compare with the sign, so it always takes a round bracket, as in $(35, \infty)$ for $x>35$.

verdict.reason: The canonical answers (-inf,7], (-inf,6] and (1/5,inf) always put a round bracket at infinity, so the error is real and supported. The refutation is correct. (-inf,7] has the square bracket at 7 only, and [-inf,7] would wrongly claim -inf is a member. The sign rule is stated correctly. The signal is precise and will not misdiagnose. There are no ids, page numbers or review-history references.

entries.label: Infinite end written on the wrong side of the end number
entries.description: The student writes the interval that starts at the end number and runs the opposite way from the set, such as $[6, \infty)$ for $x\le6$ or $(-\infty, 35)$ for $x>35$, so the bracket suits the sign but the set lies on the other side of the number.
entries.signal: The $\infty$ is written after the end number when the sign is $<$ or $\le$, or $-\infty$ is written before it when the sign is $>$ or $\ge$, for example $[6, \infty)$ for $x\le6$.

refutation.text_md: You have the end number, and a bracket that fits the sign. What has flipped is the direction: your interval runs away from the end number the opposite way from the set.

Test it on the real numbers $x$ with $x>35$. Written the wrong way round, the interval becomes $(-\infty, 35)$. The number $100$ is bigger than $35$, so it belongs to the set, but $(-\infty, 35)$ stops at $35$ and does not hold $100$. And $0$ is inside $(-\infty, 35)$ but is not bigger than $35$. The right interval, $(35, \infty)$, holds $100$ and leaves out $0$.

Read the sign as a word. $<$ or $\le$ means smaller than the end number, so the set heads down towards $-\infty$. $>$ or $\ge$ means bigger, so it heads up towards $\infty$. In an interval the smaller end is written first and the larger end last, as in $(-5, 5)$ and $[21, 41)$, so $-\infty$ always comes first and $\infty$ always comes last.

Before you write the interval, ask whether the set holds numbers smaller or bigger than the end number. Smaller: start with $-\infty$, as in $(-\infty, 7]$ for $x\le7$. Bigger: finish with $\infty$, as in $(35, \infty)$ for $x>35$. Then pick the bracket for the end number from the sign, and check with one number from the set.

verdict.reason: I checked this against ex6-1-1c and ex6-1-2a. The refutation's counter-test is correct. With x>35, 100 belongs to the set but not to (-inf,35), and 0 is in (-inf,35) but not in the set. The rule that < or <= heads to -inf and > or >= heads to inf, with the smaller end written first, matches the canonical intervals. The signal is accurate, and the step-4 examples (-inf,7] and (35,inf) are canonical forms. There are no forbidden references.

entries.label: Expects the input to appear in the answer of a constant function
entries.description: For a function like k(x) = 3 the student expects the number put in to show up in the answer, so they multiply by it or copy it instead of giving the constant.
entries.signal: k(100) given as 300 or 100 instead of 3

refutation.text_md: You are expecting the number you put in to show up in the answer, so $k(100)$ becomes something like $3\times 100=300$, or just $100$. That instinct is right for most functions: the input usually changes the output.

But look at the rule $k(x)=3$. To evaluate a function you replace each $x$ on the right-hand side with the input, and here there is no $x$ on the right-hand side to replace. Nothing carries the 100 into the answer.
Compare $g(x)=x-4$. It does contain $x$, so $g(-7)=(-7)-4=-11$ depends on the input. A 300 would only appear from a rule like $3x$, which is not the rule you were given.
The book says it directly: whatever value of $x$ you use, the output of $k$ is always 3. Even in $k(f(6))$, after $f(6)=(6)^2+1=37$ goes in, $k(37)=3$ and the answer is still 3.
Next time, read the right-hand side of the rule first. If the input letter is not there, the answer is simply the number that is there. If it is there, replace the letter with your input.

entries.label: Puts a given output in as the input
entries.description: When a question gives the answer the function produces and asks for the input, the student evaluates the function at that given number instead of setting the function equal to it and solving.
entries.signal: 4083 (or R4083) for how many litres of petrol R300 buys

refutation.text_md: You treated R300 as the input, as if it were the number of litres, and worked out $P(300)=13.61(300)=4083$. Your evaluating is correct: multiplying by 13.61 is exactly how $P$ works. The slip is in which number is the input.
Check with a case you can read: $P(8)=13.61(8)=\text{R}108.88$. The 8 in the brackets is litres, and what comes out is rand. So $P(300)$ would be the cost of 300 litres, R4083, a long way above R300.

In this question R300 is money, so it is the output of $P$, not the input. The question asks which input gives that output, so, as the book does, write the output on one side: $P(V)=300$, which means $13.61V=300$.
Now the unknown is the input $V$, and you solve for it: $V=\frac{300}{13.61}=22.043$ litres.
Next time, decide whether the number you are given is an input (it goes in the brackets) or an output (it is the answer). If it is an output, set the function equal to it and solve for the input.

entries.label: Applies the functions of a composition in the wrong order
entries.description: In a composition such as f(g(1)) the student applies the function written first to the number first, instead of working out the inner function g(1) and feeding its answer into f.

refutation.text_md: You know how to evaluate $f$ and $g$, but you started with $f$ because it is written first. In $f(g(1))$ the number 1 is the input of $g$, not of $f$.
The brackets show the order: $g(1)$ sits inside $f(\ )$, so it has to be worked out first, and its answer becomes the input of $f$.
Doing it that way: $g(1)=(1)-4=-3$, so $f(g(1))=f(-3)=(-3)^2+1=10$. The book handles $k(f(6))$ the same way: $f(6)=37$ first, then $k(37)=3$.
Starting with $f$ instead gives $f(1)=(1)^2+1=2$ and then $g(2)=(2)-4=-2$. That answers a different question, $g(f(1))$, and it gives $-2$, not 10.
Next time, work from the innermost bracket outwards: find the inner value first, then use it as the input of the next function.

entries.label: Gives the range when asked for the domain
entries.description: Asked for the domain, the student reads the interval of function values up the vertical axis (and describes it as a distance) instead of the interval of input values along the horizontal axis.
entries.signal: The 'domain' is given as an interval of the function's own quantity, for example in metres or kilometres, when the horizontal axis is time.

refutation.text_md: You read a genuine interval off the graph, but from the wrong axis. The numbers you gave run up the vertical axis, the values of the function, and that interval is the range. The question asked for the domain.

The domain is read along the horizontal axis: the values of $t$, from where the graph starts to where it stops. The range is read up the vertical axis: the values of $s(t)$. They are two different intervals, so swapping them gives a different answer.

Take the ball rolling down a $10$ m slope, where the line runs from $(0, 10)$ to $(20, 0)$. Reading the vertical axis gives $0 \text{ m} \le s(t) \le 10 \text{ m}$, and that is the range. The domain is $0 \text{ s} \le t \le 20 \text{ s}$, the total time taken to reach the bottom of the slope. A domain that comes out in metres, when the horizontal axis is time, is a sign the vertical axis was read.

Before you read anything off, say which axis the question is about. For the domain, run along the horizontal axis and read the first and last $t$ values of the graph. For the range, run up the vertical axis and read the lowest and highest values of $s(t)$.

The axis is only the scale the picture is drawn on, and it is usually marked a little further than the graph needs. The domain and the range describe the graph itself: the values it actually covers, from its first point to its last.

In the same way the vertical axis is marked above $10$ m, but the line never rises above $10$ m, so the range is $0 \text{ m} \le s(t) \le 10 \text{ m}$.

Put your finger on the first and last points of the graph itself, including an end dot if there is one. Read their $t$ values for the domain and their $s$ values for the range, and ignore any empty axis beyond them.

entries.label: Assuming the graph must have a $y$-intercept
entries.description: The student puts $x=0$ into the hyperbola's equation but does not stop at the fraction with 0 on the bottom, so they say a $y$-intercept exists (or that the substitution has a solution) instead of concluding there is none.

refutation.text_md: You started in the right place: a $y$-intercept is found by putting $x=0$ into the equation. The slip is expecting that step to always hand you a point, so you said a $y$-intercept exists without checking what the fraction does when $x=0$.

Look at what happens. In $y=\frac{3}{x}+2$, putting in $x=0$ gives $y=\frac{3}{(0)}+2$. A fraction with 0 on the bottom is undefined: it has no value at all, not even 0. There is nothing to add 2 to, so no value of $y$ comes out. The substitution has no solution, which is why $(0, 2)$ is not a point on this graph.

This is the same fact that gives the domain. An equation like $y=\frac{2}{x}+2$ is undefined only at $x=0$, so its domain is $\{x: x\in\mathbb{R}, x\ne0\}$. A $y$-intercept is a point of the graph where $x=0$. If $x=0$ is not allowed, there is no such point, so the graph never meets the $y$-axis.

So the answer is that there is no $y$-intercept. Next time, put $x=0$ into the equation and look at the fraction. If it ends up with 0 on the bottom, write "undefined" and conclude there is no $y$-intercept. Try that on your own equation now.

The slip is that two different jobs for a line have got joined together: a line the curves creep towards (an asymptote) is not the same as a line the graphs are reflected about (an axis of symmetry).

Find the line the pair is reflected about first. $(1, 2)$ is on $y=2^x$ and $(-1, 2)$ is on $y=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x$. They are at the same height on opposite sides of the $y$-axis. That is why $y=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x$ is the reflection of $y=2^x$ about the $y$-axis. So the line of symmetry for this pair is the $y$-axis, not the $x$-axis.

Now test the $x$-axis as an axis of symmetry. That would need part of the graph on the other side of it, matching the part above. Every value of $2^x$ and of $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x$ is positive (the range is $y>0$), so both graphs lie completely above the $x$-axis. Nothing sits below it to be a reflection.

What the $x$-axis does instead is this. For $y=2^x$, as $x$ goes $-1, -2$ the values go $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}$: closer to $0$ each time, never reaching it. For $y=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x$, as $x$ goes $1, 2$ the values go $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}$: the same thing. Both graphs approach the $x$-axis but never touch it, and a line like that is an asymptote. The answer is A, asymptote.

Next time, ask two questions of a line. Do the graphs get closer and closer to it without touching it? Then it is an asymptote. Is one graph the reflection of the other about it? Then it is the axis of symmetry. For $y=b^x$ and $y=\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^x$, the $x$-axis is the asymptote $y=0$ for both, and the $y$-axis is the line the pair is reflected about.

(1,2) is on 2^x and (-1,2) is on (1/2)^x, so the pair mirrors about the y-axis, which matches the book's 'reflection about the y-axis'. The range y>0 means both graphs sit above the x-axis, so nothing can mirror across it. The values 1/2, 1/4 get closer to 0 and never reach it, so the x-axis (y=0) is an asymptote, as in we12. The refutation argues against the conflation rather than restating the method, and it names no question id, page, figure or review history. The canonical text of ex6-5-6a says the asymptote is x=0, which contradicts ex6-5-6b, we12 and ex6-8-50e. The refutation does not repeat that and follows the other three.

entries.label: Reads 'larger base, steeper graph' as 'larger base, higher graph'
entries.description: The student remembers that a larger base makes a steeper graph and turns it into 'the graph with the largest base is the highest everywhere', so at a negative x-value they pick the graph with the largest base.
entries.signal: Picks the increasing graph with the largest base (such as $y=3^{x}$ rather than $y=2^{x}$) as the highest graph at a negative x-value.

refutation.text_md: You are remembering something true: for $y=k^{x}$ with $k>1$, the greater the value of $k$, the steeper the curve. But steeper describes how fast the curve climbs as $x$ increases. It does not say the curve is higher at every $x$-value.
Test it with a table of values at $x=-2$. $2^{-2}=\frac{1}{4}$ and $3^{-2}=\frac{1}{9}$. The graph with the larger base is the lower one here, not the higher one.

All these graphs pass through $(0, 1)$. To the right of that point the larger base is higher ($2^{2}=4$ but $3^{2}=9$). To the left of it, the larger base gives the smaller value, so its curve is lower and closer to the $x$-axis. Which graph is higher depends on which side of the $y$-axis you are on.

So never decide from the size of the base alone. Substitute the $x$-value you are asked about into every equation, write the values in a table, and compare the numbers. The biggest number belongs to the highest graph.

verdict.reason: The error is a plausible stretching of the book's true statement that a greater k gives a steeper curve. Every computation checks out: 2^-2=1/4 and 3^-2=1/9, and 2^2=4 and 3^2=9. entries.label: Chooses an increasing graph as the highest one at a negative x-value

refutation.text_md: You noticed something right: to the left of the $y$-axis the order of the increasing graphs swaps, so $2^{x}$ is above $3^{x}$. Every increasing graph passes through $(0, 1)$ and, going left, falls towards the $x$-axis, which is its asymptote. So at a negative $x$-value an increasing graph always has a $y$-value less than 1: here $\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{9}$.

The graphs of the form $\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{x}$ are reflections of the increasing graphs about the $y$-axis, so they do the opposite: to the left of the $y$-axis they lie above 1. At $x=-2$, $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}=2^{2}=4$.

$\frac{1}{4}$ is far below 4, so an increasing graph cannot be the highest at $x=-2$. Before you choose, fill in a table of values for every graph at that $x$-value, including the decreasing ones, and compare all the numbers. The biggest value is the highest graph.

entries.label: Mixes up the reflection in the x-axis and the reflection in the y-axis
entries.description: The student puts the minus sign in the wrong place: on the exponent for a reflection in the x-axis, or on the whole function for a reflection in the y-axis.
entries.signal: For $f(x)=3^{x}$, gives $3^{-x}$ for the reflection in the x-axis, or $-3^{x}$ for the reflection in the y-axis.

refutation.text_md: You know a reflection brings a minus sign into the equation, and you put it in one of the two possible places. The only slip is which place belongs to which axis.

Use two points of $f(x)=3^{x}$: $(0, 1)$ and $(2, 9)$. A reflection in the x-axis keeps each x and flips each y, so $(2, 9)$ goes to $(2, -9)$. A reflection in the y-axis keeps each y and flips each x, so $(2, 9)$ goes to $(-2, 9)$.

Test $-3^{x}$. At $x=2$ it gives $-3^{2}=-9$, so it passes through $(2, -9)$ and is the reflection in the x-axis. At $x=-2$ it gives $-3^{-2}=-\frac{1}{9}$, not 9, so it cannot be the reflection in the y-axis.

Test $3^{-x}$. At $x=-2$ it gives $3^{2}=9$, so it passes through $(-2, 9)$ and is the reflection in the y-axis. At $x=2$ it gives $3^{-2}=\frac{1}{9}$, not $-9$, so it cannot be the reflection in the x-axis.

So the reflection in the x-axis changes the sign of the whole function, $h(x)=-3^{x}$. The reflection in the y-axis changes the sign of the exponent, $g(x)=3^{-x}$. To be sure, reflect one known point and test your equation on it.

verdict.reason: Canonical: x-axis reflection gives -3^x (or -4^x), y-axis reflection gives 3^{-x}. The refutation reflects (2,9) to (2,-9) for the x-axis and to (-2,9) for the y-axis. -3^x gives -9 at x=2 and -1/9 at x=-2. 3^{-x} gives 9 at x=-2 and 1/9 at x=2. The arithmetic and the conclusion both check out and match the canonical answers. It argues against the swap with a point test, not just by restating the rule. entries.label: Swaps a vertical stretch and a vertical shift
entries.description: The student adds the number for a vertical stretch, or multiplies by the number for a vertical shift, instead of putting the stretch in $a$ and the shift in $q$.
entries.signal: For $f(x)=3^{x}$, gives $3^{x}+2$ where a vertical stretch by 2 is asked, or $-3\cdot3^{x}$ where a vertical shift by $-3$ is asked.

refutation.text_md: You picked up the right numbers, but each one is doing the other's job. The slip is which part of $y=a\cdot b^{x}+q$ each number belongs in.
In $y=a\cdot b^{x}+q$, the number $a$ multiplies the whole power, so it is the vertical stretch. The number $q$ is added at the end, so it is the vertical shift, and it moves the asymptote.

Take $f(x)=3^{x}$, with its asymptote at $y=0$ and points $(0, 1)$ and $(2, 9)$. A vertical stretch by 2 multiplies the whole power: $j(x)=2\cdot3^{x}$. Its asymptote stays at $y=0$ and the points become $(0, 2)$ and $(2, 18)$. Adding 2 instead, $3^{x}+2$, would move the asymptote up to $y=2$ and give $(0, 3)$ and $(2, 11)$. That is a shift, not a stretch.

A vertical shift by $-3$ is added at the end: $k(x)=3^{x}-3$. The asymptote moves down to $y=-3$ and $(0, 1)$ becomes $(0, -2)$. Multiplying by $-3$ instead, $-3\cdot3^{x}$, would turn the curve upside down and leave the asymptote at $y=0$.
Next time: a stretch changes $a$, so multiply the whole $3^{x}$. A shift changes $q$, so add or subtract a number at the end.

verdict.reason: Canonical: a vertical stretch by 2 gives j=2·3^x, a shift by -3 gives k=3^x-3, and a shift up by 1 gives 4^x+1. The refutation's numbers all check. For 2·3^x the points are (0,2) and (2,18) with the asymptote at y=0. For 3^x+2 they are (0,3) and (2,11) with the asymptote at y=2. For 3^x-3, (0,1) goes to (0,-2) with the asymptote at y=-3. For -3·3^x the curve is upside down with the asymptote at y=0. It ties a to the stretch and q to the shift of the asymptote, as in y=ab^x+q. It argues against the swap and not only the method. No forbidden references. The signal (3^x+2 for a stretch, -3·3^x for a shift) matches the real error.

entries.label: Gives a the wrong sign for the side of the asymptote the point lies on
entries.description: The student finds the size of $a$ correctly but loses its sign, so the curve described lies on the wrong side of its asymptote.
entries.signal: The size of $a$ is right and the sign is wrong, for example $a=1$ with $q=4$ for a curve that levels off along $y=4$ and passes through $(-3, 3.875)$, where $a=-1$ is right.

refutation.text_md: You found the size of $a$ correctly and lost its sign. That is easy to do when the arithmetic comes out as $0.125$ divided by $0.125$. The sign of $a$ tells you which side of the asymptote the curve is on.

Take a curve $y=a\cdot2^{x}+q$ with its asymptote at $y=4$ that passes through $(-3, 3.875)$. So $q=4$, and $3.875-4=a\cdot2^{-3}$. The left side is $-0.125$, not $0.125$, because the point lies below the asymptote.

Now $-0.125=0.125a$ gives $a=-1$. If you used $a=1$, the curve $y=2^{x}+4$ would give $0.125+4=4.125$ at $x=-3$. That is above the asymptote, not the $3.875$ we were given. With $a=-1$ you get $-0.125+4=3.875$, which fits.
This works because $2^{x}$ is always positive, so $a\cdot2^{x}$ has the same sign as $a$. A positive $a$ keeps the curve above $y=q$. A negative $a$ puts it below $y=q$.

Next time: once you have $q$, compare the y-value of the given point with $q$. Below $q$ means $a$ is negative, above $q$ means $a$ is positive. Then put your $a$ and $q$ back into the point to check.

verdict.reason: Re-solved: with q=4, 3.875-4=-0.125 and -0.125=0.125a gives a=-1, matching canonical ex6-5-2. a=1 would give 4.125 at x=-3, above the asymptote, which fits neither the point nor the canonical answer. a=-1 gives 3.875. The claim that 2^x>0, so the sign of a sets the side of the asymptote, is correct and falls under the objective's 'sign of a' effect. The check 'compare the point's y with q' is sound. The refutation addresses the sign slip specifically, with a concrete counterexample. No forbidden references. The signal (right size, wrong sign, a=1 with q=4) is diagnostic.

entries.description: The student writes a square bracket at $q$, such as $[q, \infty)$, as if the graph reached the line $y = q$, when it only gets closer and closer to it.

Next time, ask: can $ab^x + q$ ever equal $q$? That would need $ab^x = 0$, which never happens. So write a round bracket at $q$: $(q, \infty)$ or $(-\infty, q)$.

entries.label: Takes $y = 0$ as the boundary and ignores $q$

refutation.text_md: You have the key fact: $b^x$ is always positive, so the graph stays on one side of a line. The slip is stopping there. The line is $y = 0$ only when $q = 0$, as in $y = 2^x$, whose range is $(0, \infty)$.

Next time, finish the chain: start with $b^x > 0$, bring in $a$, then add $q$ to both sides. The last line tells you the boundary, $y = q$.

entries.label: Chooses the side of $y = q$ without using the sign of $a$
entries.description: The student finds $q$ but puts the range on the wrong side of $y = q$: either the same side whatever the sign of $a$, or $(-\infty, q)$ for a positive $a$ and $(q, \infty)$ for a negative $a$.
entries.signal: The range lies on the wrong side of $y = q$ for the sign of $a$, for example $(q, \infty)$ when $a$ is negative, or the same range is given for $y = ab^x + q$ and $y = -ab^x + q$.

Start from what is always true: $b^x > 0$. When $a$ is positive, $ab^x$ is also positive, and adding $q$ gives $ab^x + q > q$. For $g(x) = 5\cdot2^x + 1$ this is $g(x) > 1$, above the line.

Check with one point. $y = 2^x$ passes through $(0, 1)$, which is above $0$, so its range cannot be $(-\infty, 0)$. $y = -2^x$ passes through $(0, -1)$, which is below $0$, so its range cannot be $(0, \infty)$.
Next time, ask first: is $a$ positive or negative? Positive means the graph lies above $y = q$, so the range is $(q, \infty)$. Negative means below, so the range is $(-\infty, q)$.

The range of 2^x is (0,inf) and of -2^x is (-inf,0), both from the book. refutation.text_md: You are using the sign of $a$ to decide: a positive $a$ keeps the graph above the x-axis and a negative $a$ keeps it below, so it never reaches $y=0$. Check it the way you find a y-intercept: let $x=0$. The $b^{x}$ part becomes $1$, so $y$ is $a$ plus the number at the end, and both count. In $y=\frac{1}{4}\cdot 4^{x}-1$, $a$ is positive, yet at $x=0$ we get $\frac{1}{4}\cdot 1-1=-0.75$, which is below the x-axis.

Both of those graphs do reach the x-axis. Letting $y=0$ gives the x-intercept $(1, 0)$ for the first and $(1.3, 0)$, to one decimal place, for the second.
So never rule out an x-intercept from the sign of $a$ alone. Let $y=0$, get the $b^{x}$ part on its own, and try values of $x$ to see whether one fits.
